claims.text: The target alloy is HfZrTiTa0.53, and processing will not alter its chemical composition.
As-cast or arc-melted HfZrTiTa0.53 has a reported yield strength of 786 MPa.
As-cast or arc-melted HfZrTiTa0.53 has a reported compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
The reported 13.5% terminal strain for HfZrTiTa0.53 is primarily a compression result.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has favorable energetic release under impact.
A 1–2 hour treatment near 1300 K followed by warm working at 950–1050 K and partial recrystallization will refine and heterogenize the grain structure of HfZrTiTa0.53.
The treatment will produce partially recrystallized grains, refined subgrains, and stable internal boundaries.
A refined heterogeneous microstructure will distribute dislocation activity and delay strain localization.
Microstructural refinement and internal boundaries will enhance uniform slip and back-stress hardening.
Enhanced uniform slip and back-stress hardening will reduce slip concentration and improve tensile work-hardening capacity.
The treatment will increase both uniform and total tensile elongation by at least 30% relative to 13.5%.
The treated alloy will retain a yield strength of at least approximately 786 MPa.
The treated alloy will retain a compressive strength near 1300 MPa.
The treated alloy will retain impact-triggered energy release comparable to the untreated alloy.
The proposed behavior is applicable from room temperature to approximately 1073 K.
The proposed behavior is applicable under quasi-static through intermediate strain rates of approximately 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1.
Annealing above 1400 K or for extended times may cause grain growth that negates strengthening.
Excessive annealing may degrade the energetic properties of HfZrTiTa0.53.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires at least a 30% increase over 13.5%, corresponding to at least 17.55%, whereas the falsification rule only requires the treated alloy to exceed 13.5%. A result between 13.5% and 17.55% would fail the quantitative prediction but would not falsify the hypothesis under the stated rule.

A terminal strain reported largely from compression is used as the numerical baseline and falsification threshold for tensile uniform elongation, although these are different loading modes and different strain metrics.
